response.sql:
WITH counts_by_gender AS (
  SELECT 
    c.gender,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) as count
  FROM Invoices i
  JOIN Orders o ON i.order_id = o.order_id
  JOIN Customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
  GROUP BY c.gender
),
with_stats AS (
  SELECT 
    gender,
    count,
    count * 1.0 / SUM(count) OVER () as share,
    1.0 / COUNT(*) OVER () as avg_share
  FROM counts_by_gender
)
SELECT 
  gender,
  count,
  share,
  share - avg_share as above_average
FROM with_stats
WHERE share > avg_share
ORDER BY share DESC;

assumptions.assumption: "Invoiced orders" means distinct orders that appear in the Invoices table (an order is counted once regardless of how many invoices reference it)
NULL values in the gender column are treated as a valid gender category and included in the grouping and average calculation

alternatives.interpretation: Count invoices instead of distinct orders: if an order has multiple invoices, each invoice counts separately rather than treating the order as a single unit

  SELECT 
    c.gender,

SELECT

  share - avg_share as above_average
FROM with_stats
WHERE share > avg_share
ORDER BY share DESC;
